An intense late season storm moved out of the central Pacific toward southern Alaska on the morning of the 5th. By 1000 ADT the low was about 300 miles south of Kodiak Island with a central pressure of 975 mb. Ships in the southern quadrant of this low recorded sustained winds from 40 to 60 knots. Portions of Kodiak Island recorded peak wind gusts of 35 to 43 knots.

An intense summer storm, with a central pressure of 979 mb, tracked west of Nikolski and into the southern Bering Sea late on the 25th. This low pushed a strong occluded front across the eastern Aleutians and Alaska Peninsula on the evening of the 25th, then into Bristol Bay early on the 26th. Strongest winds were reported from Cold Bay with a peak gust of 60 knots at 2233 and 2244 AST on the 25th. For a 3-hour period Cold Bay received sustained winds of 40 to 45 knots. Both Dutch Harbor and Port Heiden had 50 knot gusts. St. Paul recorded a peak gust of 39 knots at 2126 AST on the 25th. Gusts of 30 to 45 knots were seen along the Bristol Bay coast, where Cape Newenham recorded 44 knots.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Although river stages never really went below flood stage along the Mississippi River for an extended period of time, levels began to increase again dramatically toward the last half of the month. Flood levels were expected to reach near record levels toward the end of the month with hundreds of buildings damaged and most crops planted in flood plains underwater. Damage was primarily agricultural since most levees protecting the counties held through June. However, at Grafton, Illinois, near the confluence of the Illinois and Mississippi Rivers, numerous homes and businesses were flooded. The Mississippi River at Grafton had been above flood stage from March 25 through June 2. It dropped below flood stage for 4 days, before rising again on June 6. It stayed above flood through the rest of the month. Flooding continued into July.

One-half mile south of Prairieton, a small plane which was anchored to the ground was lifted into the air and thrown into a tree.
Trees were downed in Shakamak State Park.
Trees were downed in Shakamak State Park.
Hail destroyed several hundred acres of corn.

The tornado destroyed a mobile home near the initial touchdown site, and injured a man who was inside asleep when it hit. The tornado also downed trees, damaged or destroyed several barns and farm buildings, and toppled chimneys and ripped siding from houses.
Trees were downed, a storage building was destroyed, and a mobile home was rolled over.
The roof was blown off of a barn.
Trees and power lines were downed, with some roads blocked by trees in the Wilbur area.
Trees were downed across the county.

Winds of 74 mph were measured 2 miles northwest of Sullivan, at the Sullivan County Airport. A small barn was blown down on Miner's City Road near Farmersburg, power lines were downed throughout much of the county, and trees were downed in the Fairbanks area.
Hail broke car and house windows.
Trees were downed, and one building was damaged.
Trees were downed southwest of Franklin.
Trees and power lines were downed in the Coal City and Patricksburg areas. A building was shifted off its foundation in Coal City, and homes were damaged in the Patricksburg area.
Trees and power lines were downed in the northern part of the county.
Trees and power lines were downed, and several homes were damaged.
Trees and power lines were downed in the Elletsville area. One person was injured when a tree fell on a car.
Large limbs were downed.
A tornado briefly touched down, and uprooted several trees and downed power lines.

Downburst wind occurred in Browning Camp between Versailles and Elrod. Several mobile homes and recreational vehicles were severely damaged when they were rolled by the winds, or when nearby trees fell on them. Downed trees also blocked several roads.

A tornado produced a short and narrow damage path through Elrod. Many outbuildings, barns, and mobile homes were destroyed. Many houses and businesses were severely damaged. A large fuel tank weighing several tons was moved about 100 yards. Four of the six injuries occurred inside a mobile home.

Downburst winds caused extensive damage near Dillsboro. Many trees fell on houses and vehicles. Three homes were severely damaged. Several outbuildings and barns were also damaged just west of Dillsboro.
An elementary school roof was damaged near Dillsboro.
Numerous trees were downed, with many trees falling on houses or automobiles.
Numerous large trees were uprooted across the southern part of the county.
Large hail damaged a police car between Troy and Tell City. Numerous automobiles and homes were damaged in the Tell City area.
Trees and limbs were blown down at County Roads 600 West and 700 North.
Trees and limbs were blown down across County Road 200 East and Evergreen Road in southwest Whitley County.
Trees and limbs were downed in western Allen County, and downed lines caused numerous power outages.
One-inch-diameter hail fell in the western part of the county.
A woman working at a nursery was injured when lightning struck a metal shelf she was touching.
A house near Howe sustained $40,000 in fire damage after it was struck by lightning.
A woman was injured by lightning after it traveled through the phone lines, leapt from the phone and hit her where she was sitting nearby.
The second floor of a two-story home was destroyed by fire after the house was struck by lightning.

Rain of 5.00 to 8.00 inches occurred from June 7 to June 8 over parts of northern Indiana. This resulted in near major flooding along some rivers during the second week of June. Extensive flooding occurred along the Elkhart, the St. Joseph, and the upper portion of the Kankakee Rivers. Flooding affected many local roads and city streets in the cities of Goshen, Elkhart, Mishawaka, and South Bend. Levees along the Kankakee River in southern LaPorte County were overtopped. Serious flooding also occurred along Pine Lake in LaPorte, where high lake levels flooded several homes.
Siding was ripped from the side of a house in Hammond.
Automobiles were damaged by hail in North Manchester.
Three-quarter-inch diameter hail fell in northwest Huntington County just south of the Whitley County line.

In New Haven, a 15-year-old male was critically injured by lightning as he was leaning against a metal construction bin in an open unfinished garage. The youth was hospitalized, but he died about a week later. Two other males were injured when they were struck by lightning in Fort Wayne. (M150)

One-inch-diameter hail damaged automobiles and crops in Ossian. Baseball-size hail damaged homes, automobiles, and crops from Markle to Tocsin. Numerous windows were broken out. The hail caused extensive damage at the Norwell School, where holes were punched in the roof.
Hail damaged automobiles in Decatur.

Downburst winds produced a swath of damage along County Road 200 West from near Williams to 1 mile south of Williams. Damage included a pickup truck overturned and destroyed, a home roof blown off, a 20-by 30-foot barn destroyed, siding damage to a number of homes, and large trees and telephone poles downed. One tree fell on a house and caused major damage.
Power poles and lines were downed in the northern part of the county.
Trees and lines were downed.
Several houses were damaged by wind and falling trees. Two houses sustained major damage with the roof being blown from one, and a large tree falling on another.

Trees were downed in Morocco, Mount Ayr, and near Roselawn. Falling trees damaged two houses in Morocco and totaled three cars. Part of a wall collapsed at the North Newton Junior-Senior High School, and caused substantial damage to a greenhouse.
A waterspout was reported at Indiana Harbor.
Numerous trees were downed across the county.
Trees were downed north of Williamsport.
Winds of 60 mph were reported just south of LaPorte. Trees and lines were downed in the Kingsbury area.
A small tornado briefly touched down, but caused no damage.
The path of the tornado was intermittent, with only sporadic damage noted. The tornado downed trees and telephone poles, and ripped the roof from a barn.

The path of the tornado was intermittent. Numerous trees and power lines were downed, the roof was blown from a barn, and the roof of a silo was blown off. There was extensive damage at the Shady Lane Campground and Mobile Home Park southwest of Plymouth. At this location one mobile home was crushed by a falling tree, and at least two cars were damaged by falling trees. The roof was also blown from a house near Plymouth. Total damage was estimated between $90,000 and $100,000.
Winds were estimated at 60 to 80 mph.

In Goshen, two people were injured when strong winds blew out the windows in a restaurant. Trees downed in the Goshen area damaged vehicles and houses. Extensive damage occurred at the fairgrounds east of Goshen where one building was destroyed, and several others were damaged. Damage at the fairgrounds totaled more than $75,000.
A small tornado briefly touched down.
Trees were downed and the roof was blown from a house on the north side of Dewart Lake.
Trees were downed near Peru.
Large trees were downed across the county.
Large trees were downed. One tree fell on a car and caused major damage.
Large trees were downed at County Road 300 West and Orland Road on the north side of Angola.
Trees and power lines were downed. Several cars were damaged by falling trees and limbs.
Numerous trees were blown down across the county.
Trees were downed on the east side of Indianapolis. Part of a roof was also blown off a building.
A barn collapsed, and about 30 homes were damaged. Trees, power lines and power poles were also downed.
Trees were downed in Mohawk. Two tractor-trailer rigs were blown off Interstate 70 near Mount Comfort.
The state police estimated winds in excess of 60 mph. The roof was blown off a mobile home.
The roof was blown off a building.
Winds were estimated at 60 mph by the county sheriff.
Trees and power lines were downed, a house was damaged, and a barn was destroyed.
Windows were blown out of a house west of Rushville. Trees were downed in Rushville, with one tree falling on a house.
A house near Hagerstown was damaged by fire after it was struck by lightning.
Several large trees were blown down around Chandler.
Several streams and creeks rose out of their banks as nearly 2.50 inches of rain fell in less than 0.5 hour. Some roads and low areas were flooded.
Several trees and power lines were blown down around the county.
Several large trees were uprooted.
Several large trees were uprooted.

Nearly stationary thunderstorms produced heavy rain which resulted in flash flooding in the Michigantown and Frankfort areas. State Roads 28 and 29 in the central part of the county were flooded, and 2 feet of water flooded parts of Frankfort.
Numerous trees were downed, and a house was damaged when a tree fell on it. Power lines were also knocked down.
Numerous trees were uprooted along and east of Highway 69 from New Harmony to Mt. Vernon.
A garage was destroyed by fire after it was hit by lightning.
A school near Goshen had part of its roof blown off.
Trees were downed by Thunderstorm wind.
Lightning started a fire that destroyed a tool shed near Fowler. Two tractors, wagons, a hay baler, a log splitter, two riding mowers, and other equipment were lost in the fire.
Numerous trees were downed, and three houses were heavily damaged by falling trees.
A man who was using a metal pole to clean a pool was injured by lightning.
Hail ranging in size from 0.75 to 1.00 inch in diameter damaged crops in the Point Isabel, Normal and Van Buren areas.
Golfball-size hail was reported in Alexandria, and trees were downed just north of Orestes.
Sixty-mph winds were measured at the Delaware County Airport. The roof was blown off of a health care center, and 35 people had to be evacuated.
On the south side of Muncie lightning hit a house, but caused little damage.
In Hagerstown, trees were downed.
The roof was blown off a building.
Trees were downed, and the roof was blown off a barn.
Three-quarter-inch hail was reported along State Route 39 north of Lebanon.
Cars were damaged by falling trees. The roof was ripped off a two-story brick building and blown into a used car lot, where it damaged two pickup trucks, and crushed a mini-van.
Trees were downed.
Trees and power lines were downed, mainly in the southern part of the county.
Trees were blown down in the southern part of the county.
A wind gust of 62 mph was measured 1.5 miles south-southwest of downtown Indianapolis. In Indianapolis a tree fell on a garage, and another tree fell on a house.
Flash flooding occurred after 1.50 to 2.00 inches of rain fell within 0.5 hour. Several roads and culverts were washed out, and a bridge near Quakerstown was damaged.
Trees were downed in Brick Chapel...
...and a tool shed was blown down 2 miles south of Bainbridge.
Trees were downed by Thunderstorm wind.
Hail fell near Ossian, and damaged several automobiles.
Numerous trees were downed in the Versailles area, and several roofs were blown off homes.
In Waldron, trees were downed by Thunderstorm wind.
Trees and power lines were downed.
Three-quarter-inch hail fell southwest of Martinsville...
...and trees were downed in Centerton.
Several trees and power lines were downed on the north side of Batesville.
Numerous trees were downed across the county.
Trees were downed in the northeastern part of the county.
Numerous trees were downed in the Bloomington area, a flag pole was blown down, and a silo was damaged.
Trees were downed by Thunderstorm wind.

Two to four inches of rain fell within a 1-hour period, and caused widespread flash flooding. The most extensive flooding occurred along Jack's Defeat Creek in the Elletsville and Stinesville areas. Several motorists became stranded and had to be rescued. In Elletsville, water levels climbed to 2 to 3 feet on State Route 46, and about 60 houses were damaged by flood waters. Six families in Elletsville had to be evacuated from their homes. In Stinesville flooding prompted the evacuation of two families. A total of about 75 houses were damaged county wide by the flooding.
Several large trees were downed.
Several large trees were downed.
Several large trees were downed.
Numerous trees were downed across the county.
Several large trees were downed in and around Rising Sun.
Trees were downed on numerous roads across the county, and power lines were downed in Vevay.

In Dearborn and Ohio Counties flash flooding closed most secondary roads near Friendship Creek. Several people in the southeast part of Dearborn County were trapped in the their homes by rising water.
In Ohio County some roads were also closed by high water in Rising Sun.

In Ripley County, 3.50 inches of rain fell between 1445 and 1645 EST. Friendship Creek in the southeast part of the county rose out of its banks, forcing officials to evacuate local camp grounds. High water closed many roads in the Versailles and Batesville areas.
In Switzerland County, several roads and culverts were washed out.
Trees were downed, and porches and roofs of several houses were damaged.
Trees were downed by Thunderstorm wind.
Trees were downed across the county.

Many roads east and south of Greensburg were flooded, and some vehicles were stranded in high water. South of Greensburg, two bridges were washed out, one along Harris City Road, and another along Millhousen Road.
Numerous large trees were blown down. Power lines were also knocked down, and one tree damaged a carport.
Power poles were downed, and several buildings were damaged.
Numerous trees were downed, mainly in the southern part of the county. A 15- by 20-foot section of roof was blown from a vacant restaurant and grocery store at Rays Crossing.
Trees were downed south of Columbus.
About 10,000 acres of corn and soybeans were damaged. There was also widespread damage to vehicles and houses.
In Burlington, 60-mph winds were reported and hail caused damage to 9,000 acres of corn and soybeans near Pittsburg through Bringhurst to Burlington.
Power lines and trees were downed at County Roads 300 North and 650 East in northern Wells County.
Hail damaged several automobiles in Fairmount.
A house near Americus was damaged by fire after being struck by lightning.
In Osgood, trees were downed by Thunderstorm wind.
Golfball-size hail fell in the southern part of the county, while 0.75-inch diameter hail covered the ground 6 inches deep in the western part of the county.
Trees were downed in the western part of the county.

Numerous trees were downed in the northeast and eastern parts of the county, and the roofs were ripped from several barns. Especially hard hit were the Guion, Judson and Hollandsburg areas. At Turkey Run State Park one tree crushed a recreational vehicle. Numerous power poles and lines were downed around Judson. A roof was ripped from a modular home near Hollandsburg.

Hail caused extensive damage in northeast Parke County, especially in the Guion, Judson, and Hollandsburg areas. Hail ranged in size from 0.50 inch in diameter to 1.75 inches in diameter. The hail damaged houses, farm buildings, vehicles, and crops. The hail damaged or destroyed 8,000 acres of corn, 6,500 acres of soybeans, 1,000 acres of wheat, 3,250 acres of mixture hay, 2,000 acres of alfalfa hay and 2,250 acres of woodland were also damaged. Several inches of hail covered the ground, with hail drifts of 1 to 2 feet reported in many areas. The hail covered roads and made travel extremely difficult. A 4-wheel drive county highway department truck became stuck in a hail drift, and had to be pulled out by another 4-wheel drive truck. After the hail ended dense fog settled over the area, and hampered travel for the remainder of the night. By noon the following day, there were still a few inches of hail covering the ground in the Guion area.
Trees were blown down, and golfball-size hail fell.
Thunderstorms dumped golfball- to baseball-size hail on northern Lake County. Over $1 million in damage occurred to car dealerships in Hammond.
Part of the roof was blown from a home in Portage, and 1.50-inch-diameter hail fell in Wheeler.

Rainfall up to 3.00 inches occurred over parts of northern Indiana on June 27, and this caused flooding along portions of the Kankakee River in northwest Indiana. Flooding was confined to agricultural lands.
Wind gusts to 83 mph were reported at the Anderson Municipal Airport, while winds to 60 mph were reported in Anderson. A large tree was blown down, and crashed into an apartment building.
A few power lines were knocked down in the county. At Fountain City a tree fell and crushed a car, and other large limbs fell on a house and crushed a playhouse.
Power lines were downed north of Sullivan, and numerous trees were downed across the county.
Numerous large trees were uprooted.
Numerous large trees were uprooted.
Rainfall during the spring of 1993 was copious and excessive...
Lightning struck a house in Milford, starting a small fire.
The first storms produced a 65 mph wind gust near Arnolds Park. The winds lifted boats from their moorings and overturned a couple of them.

Heavy rainfall during the morning of the 7th, combined with additional rainfall that developed by mid afternoon resulted in flash flooding in the county. Many creeks and streams overflowed their banks as upwards of 3.00 inches of rain fell in a short period, less than 2 hours, of time.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As the low mentioned above continued to move northeast, the warm front pressed into Iowa and a dry line moved across the plains. Thunderstorms fired ahead of the dry line in northwest Iowa. The storms fired from a combination of the dry line and synoptic forcing. The first storms produced a 65 mph wind gust near Arnolds Park. The winds lifted boats from their moorings and overturned a couple of them. Several tornadoes were spawned by the storms. The strongest was in Lyon and Osceola Counties. The tornado was on the ground for about 10 miles. Though much of its path was over open country, the tornado did cause significant damage in Sibley. On its path, the tornado destroyed a cattle shed, blew out windows, and downed several trees. In Sibley, one roof was taken off of a house and a high school bus barn was taken down. Damage to the bus barn was around $150,000. There were several injuries in Sibley caused by flying glass and debris. Two other were injured as the collided while driving their cars in an attempt to outrun the tornado. Ironically, the call to action statement in the tornado warning for the area specifically advised NOT to try to outrun the tornado in your car. A second tornado was on the ground for about 7.5 miles. This tornado was not as strong, but did cause damage in Sioux County between Hospers and Sheldon. Several barns were taken down, along with a few silos. The tornado moved into the campus of the Northwest Iowa Community College, causing quite a bit of damage to the buildings. Other tornadoes touched down in the area in what turned out to be a small family of tornadoes. Damage was minor as the other tornadoes swept across open countryside. Lightning struck a house in Milford, starting a small fire.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: June of 1993 was yet another cool and wet month...
High winds caused some damage in the Corydon area.
Another storm toppled several trees and power lines onto cars in the city of Clinton.
Excessive rains over Wayne and Appanoose Counties temporarily closed portions of Highway 2.
Monroe County reported road closures as well.
An example of the rain that fell during the evening of the 7th included 3.50 inches of rain in one hour at Promise City, in Wayne County.

Water was reportedly up to 3 feet deep on roads in Davis County at the peak of the flooding. Precipitation reports from Davis County indicated that 5.12 inches fell from the storms. Much of it, 3.00 to 4.00 inches, fell in less than 2 hours time.
High winds caused damage... at Bloomfield.
Heavy rainfall once again struck over Iowa causing significant river flooding. Widespread amounts in the 1.50- to 3.00-inch range fell over much of the lowa and Cedar River Basins.
Structural damage was also reported in Washington County in the Riverside area.
South of the city of Washington, high winds toppled a barn, killing 60 sows.
The storms touched off a brief tornado touch down in Boone County. During its brief life, one house was damage in the town of Fraser.
Another tornado touched down briefly at the Forest City Airport. A few buildings were damaged by this tornado.

The most significant hail occurred in Mitchell County. As was described by a local farmer there, large chunks of ice began to fall from the sky. The hail became larger and larger with some of the stones the size of softballs. Four farms in the county were badly damaged by the large hail.

A tornado was spawned by the storm southeast of the Osage area. Fortunately, it tracked across farm fields for the most part. It did strike four farmsteads, damaging one severely. Several small out buildings and barns were damaged but the farm houses were spared. On one farmstead, a pine tree was picked up and thrown over the house. A car was lifted and thrown 70 meters. Several calves and one pig were killed.
A trucker was injured on Highway 218 north of Ainsworth as high winds toppled his tractor-semitrailer.
South of this area, a small tornado touched down north of Wyman. It was on the ground for about 5 miles.
One house was damaged south of Columbus City. High winds threw a tree through the picture window of another house in Columbus City.
In Wapello, winds lifted a trailer and threw a child against a car. She was slightly injured.
Another cell became severe over Scott County. Tree damage and some power line damage occurred in Buffalo.

Urban flooding resulted from heavy rainfall in the city of Muscatine. Water was reportedly 2 feet deep for about an hour on some of the city streets. Several manhole covers were blown off from the water pressure.
Golfball-size hail fell in Buena Vista County at the onset of the storm development.
Three to six inches of rain fell in less than 2 hours in Buena Vista County, resulting in considerable flash flooding in the county.
Heavy rainfall in Cherokee County forced the closing of U.S. Highway 59 south of Cherokee for a period of time.
High winds in Onawa, in Monona County, physically moved a grain bin 75 feet from its moorings.

In what appeared to be a microburst, very strong winds blew through the Crushing area of Woodbury county. Tree branches were thrown through the window of one house. Relatives were sleeping over for the night and were on the floor. The wind pushed them across the room inside the house.
High winds blew down several trees in the northwest edge of Des Moines.
One tornado occurred in the southwest part of Iowa northeast of Red Oak. Little damage occurred as the tornado crossed open country, though it did take one trailer off of its foundation.
High winds in the Elliot area caused damage in east of Corning.

Flash Flooding occurred in Adams County from the heavy rainfall. In fact, 4.00 inches of rain fell on the town of Lenox in just one hours time. Runoff from the heavy rainfall caused rapid flooding with many bridges reported as under water for a time. In addition, there were reports of several bridges being washed out by the flash flooding.
High winds east of Mason City caused damage in the area, removing the roof from one building and destroyed one mobile home.
One of the stronger storms produced hail of 1.25 inch in diameter over the northern part of Warren County.
Two barns were destroyed north of Stanwood, in Cedar County, by microburst winds. Some large oak trees were blown down. Much of the damage was confined to a two city block size area.
South of May City, reports indicated that hail up to golfball-size had nearly completely covered the ground.
Later in the evening, lightning touched off a house fire in Milford.
Golfball-size hail fell in Clay County in the city of Webb.
High winds downed a grain silo in Palo Alto County near Ayrshire
High winds... caused damage west of Emmetsburg. A new flag pole was snapped off near Emmetsburg as well.
Significant structural damage was reported on one farmstead in Humboldt County at Bode. Minor structural damage was reported at several others around the area as well.
A tornado touched down briefly in Wright County south of the Clarion Airport. Witnesses reported seeing the tornado pick up dirt as it touched down in an open field.
Lightning struck a chimney in Ames. The force of the lightning bolt knocked bricks off of the chimney resulting in significant damage to five cars parked below.
A similar situation occurred in Fayette County in the Oelwein area. High winds ripped off the roof of a school there, causing in excess of $100,000 in damage.
In Winneshiek County, winds took off half of the junior high school roof in the town of Jackson Junction. Winds were reportedly near 85 mph. Damage to the roof was placed at $54,000.
In Allamakee County, trees and power lines were downed in the city of Waukon. Some barns were also damaged in the area.
High winds in Lansing caused roof damage to several homes in the city as winds estimated around 75 mph buffeted the city.
One thunderstorm moved through Linn County and produced high winds. The roof was blown off of a barn and a chicken house was blown off of its foundation near Palo.
Structural damage was reported in Mitchell County at Riceville as high winds swept through the town.
Several farms were damaged in Hardin County by high winds. On one of the farms several hogs were killed as a barn was destroyed near Hubbard.
One thunderstorm produced a funnel cloud in Chickasaw County for a brief period.
Another lightning strike occurred in Delaware County at Hopkinton. The lightning strike caused a small fire after striking a house there.
High winds leveled a house that was under construction north of Dyersville in Dubuque County.

The highest wind gust was a 78 mph wind gust recorded southeast of Conrad in Marshall County as one of the storms collapsed. Windows were blown out of houses there, the garage door was blown in on one house, and several light poles were toppled.
Lightning struck a house in the city of Waterloo. Minor damage occurred to the house with a small fire and damage to electrical appliances.
Other damage included... structural damage to houses in Jones County in Oxford Junction.

This rain event became the first really widespread event for the state. The rain fell over the state for an extended period of time; three days in fact... Flooding was moderate on the Iowa River above Coralville, the upper portion of the Cedar River, and the South Skunk River near Oskaloosa. General flooding, mostly minor, was recorded elsewhere around the state... Damage was difficult to estimate, but was well into the millions of dollars in terms of property losses. Crop damage was even more difficult to estimate...
Three-quarter inch diameter hail fell in Pella, for the only report of hail reaching severe criteria.
Another Cell collapsed in Butler County at Clarksville. It produced winds of 60 mph, downing several trees.
One cell collapsed east of Fairfield, resulting in high winds that downed many trees and some power lines.
Flash Flooding occurred in Marion County as 2.00 to 3.00 inches of rain fell in a 45-minute time period. Highway 5 was under 6.00 to 7.00 inches of water for a period of time.

One barn was destroyed, however the hogs in the barn were able to escape. The tornado toppled over head stones in a cemetery southwest of Sigourney. The tornado briefly lifted as it crossed highway 149, then touched down and destroyed two out buildings and tore the side off an airplane hanger at the Sigourney Airport. Extensive damage was reported at the airport.

A more significant flash flood event took place over southern Benton and northern Iowa Counties. Reports indicated that up to 3.50 inches of rain fell in a 45-minute period of time there. Flooding occurred in many basements. Two county bridges were washed out in southern Benton County and one car was washed off the road southwest of Vinton... Three were killed in this incident, a 22-year-old female, a 19-year-old female who was 7 months pregnant, and the baby. (F19V, F22V, F0V)
The flooding was not as major in northern Iowa County. Flood waters abated within a few hours.

Another occurrence of downburst winds occurred in Benton County. There were numerous reports of damage around the county, mainly over the north half. Numerous trees downed and out buildings were damaged or destroyed.
Lightning struck the Law Enforcement building in Benton County. Computer equipment was damaged inside with damage in the $2,000 to $3,000 range.

A strong tornado touched down in Delaware County. The storm was tracked by weather radar as a mesocyclone. It touched down south and west of Manchester, causing major structural damage to a farm house. Later it picked up a car, spun it around, and turned it upside down north of Manchester. It moved into a forested area and finally lifted.

The third tornado was also quite strong. It touched down south of the Dubuque Airport. Tree branches fell out of the sky onto the runway at the Dubuque Airport. A large piece of sheet metal fell on top of the terminal building. A Northwest Airlink flight landed at the airport with tree branches attached to the aircraft. At least one farmstead was hit with a glancing blow. About $15,000 damage was reported with several propane tanks leaking following the damage caused by the tornado. The tornado tracked north-northeast across the extreme northwest tip of Illinois and into southwest Wisconsin where it finally dissipated.

The most significant high wind event took place in Clayton County, where a downburst wind caused significant damage. Four farm wagons were overturned, at least one power pole was snapped, and structural damage occurred on one farmstead.

Heavy rainfall over the upper Mississippi River Basin resulted in a large river crest as it came downstream through eastern Iowa. The levels crested just below the record crests of the great floods of 1965 and 1973... Major damage occurred along the river cities and farm land... The city of Davenport was very hard hit. Much of the downtown area was under water. Severe damage occurred there... Thousands and thousands of acres of farm land were under water. Crop losses were great. In addition, many farm levees were destroyed and overtopped by the high flood waters.

Hardest hit was eastern Emmet County. Between 1430 CST and 1800 CST, between 6.00 and 8.00 inches of rain fell around the Armstrong area... By 1620 CST, water was flooding over Highway 9. An hour later, water was over two places on Highway 9, Highway 15 along the Emmet-Kossuth County line was overtopped with water, and numerous gravel roads were closed due to flash flooding.

Northern Kossuth County was affected by the flash flooding, though not to the extent that Emmet County was. Two to three inches of rain fell in a short period of time, under 2 hours, causing flash flooding.

Rainfall occurred over the northwestern part of Iowa. In the upper half of the Little Sioux River Basin, 1.50 inches of rain was reported with 1.50 to 3.00 inches falling over the south half. Flooding was minor and generally restricted to the lower part of the Little Sioux River. Much of the flooding was caused by levees and levee failure.
Lightning also struck one house in New London, setting it on fire.
The only other lightning strike reported was south of the Mt. Pleasant Airport, where lightning took down a utility pole.
One storm did produce high winds in Des Moines County at Mediapolis. About $46,000 damage was done on one farmstead when winds downed a machine building.

The most significant rainfall report came from Henry County, where a report of 6.50 inches of rainfall in 15 minutes was received from New London. Other reports from the area included 3.00 inches in Burlington, 5.00 inches in Fort Madison, and a total rainfall in New London of 10.10 inches. Many areas reported 2.00 to 3.00 inches of rainfall in under 2 hours. Flooding was widespread in Henry County due to the heavy rainfall. Numerous roads were closed and under water, with the water covering several bridges. The sheriff reported the Skunk River was out of its banks and had risen 30 inches in the 3-hour period between 1630 CST and 1930 CST. Roads and bridges along the river were going under water at that time. The town of New London reported extensive flooding with many roads blocked off.
In Des Moines County, U.S. Highway 61 had water 3 feet deep covering it in some areas south of Burlington.
In Jones County for example, heavy rainfall resulted in water running over roads in the Wyoming area at a depth of 3 feet.
Route 136 was reportedly under up to 8.00 inches of water for a 5- to 10-mile stretch.
Flash Flooding in Van Buren County was heaviest over the southeast part of the county, where many roads were overtopped with water.

General rainfall occurred over the eastern part of Iowa on the 24th and early on the 25th. Rainfall amounts were in the 1.00 to 2.00 inch range in an area from near Dubuque down toward Coralville Reservoir to Keosaqua and all areas eastward. Rainfall was generally around 3.00 inches or more along the Mississippi River. As has been the case with most of the rainfall events this month, a significant flash flooding event preceded the general flooding event. As the water from the flash floods, as mentioned above most of these, flowed into the rivers a period of general flooding followed. Moderate river flooding occurred on the lower portions of the Iowa River, especially at Wapello, and the Cedar River, especially at Conesville.
Lightning struck a power pole there, knocking out power and telephone service in the city of Greely.
Baseball-size hail covered the ground 6 miles north of Harlan.

One cell dropped hail in a swath about 2 miles wide and nearly 20 miles long. In the center of this band, the hail was anywhere from golfball to softball size... Crop damage was severe. Reports of 75 percent crop destruction were common within the hail swath.

Northwest of Little Sioux, hail up to the size of golfballs completely covered the ground. There was enough hail on the ground to for drifts of hail to form. Needless to say, crop damage in the area was significant.
A barn was damaged northwest of Massillon by the high winds. The barn was damaged and several head of cattle were killed. Trees were also uprooted in the area.

Rainfall reports of 4.00 to 6.00 inches were received around the Coralville Dam area. The Dam site officially recorded 3.60 inches of rain. There was an unofficial report of 6.00 inches just south of Iowa City. The heavy rains caused a two-fold problem. First, the ground in the area was already saturated. This caused considerable run off and closed several roads. The second problem was with the Coralville Reservoir itself. The reservoir was near capacity and the heavy rainfall nearly caused it to overflow.
High winds did cause some damage in the Buffalo area of Scott County.
There was a report of wind damage in Mills County with a few trees being downed.
Hail a little smaller than golfball size pelted the Andover area of Clinton County.

General rainfall over the 4-county area was in the 1.50- to 2.50-inch range... Reports indicated that some of the rivers in the area rose over a foot in less than 5 minutes as the runoff entered the river system. Agricultural areas reported widespread flooding.
The heaviest rainfall reported was in the Silver City area of Mills County, where 5.00 inches of rain was reported by an unofficial observer there.
Considerable street flooding was reported in Clarinda for example.

A storm collapsed in Page County over the city of Clarinda. The microburst winds caused significant damage in the city. A new bowling alley and an A & W root beer stand were damaged. A dealership in town had a significant part of its roof removed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several tornadoes were spawned during the evening. Most of them were brief touch downs and caused little damage. Such was the case in Greene County, where two brief touch downs occurred in open countryside. An earlier touch down north of Sibley, in Ocseola County, did little more than cause tree damage. Two tornadoes touched down in Pocahontas County. The first was a brief touch down. The second was on the ground between Havelock and Gilmore City. Much of the area it traversed was open country. A few farmsteads were affected with most damage to out buildings. One farmstead received significant damage northwest of Gilmore City just before the tornado lifted. The storm was still strong as it moved across the city. Damage was substantial at a lumber yard as high winds lifted the roof from the building and threw it into a house across the street. The lumber yard building was virtually destroyed it. The longest tornado track cut across three counties. The tornado touched down in Boone County and cut a path across southern Story County into northeast Polk County. This tornado had a very intermittent track and lifted several times or remained just above ground. As it moved across northeast Polk County, the storm weakened. Damage was limited due to its intermittent track and the fact that that part of the state is not heavily populated. The storm moved into Jasper County, but by then was below severe levels and just produced heavy rainfall and some small hail. During the late night hours, two tornadoes touched down in Scott County. One north of New Liberty was only a brief touch down and caused no significant damage. The second was north of the Stockton area. A couple was camping in Scott County north of Stockton. The tornado rolled their mobile home. The husband received several cuts and bruises. His wife sustained a broken arm and cuts that required 24 stitches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An earlier touch down north of Sibley, in Ocseola County, did little more than cause tree damage.
Rainfall was intense in Dickinson and Emmet Counties. During a period of 3 to 4 hours, 6.00 to 7.00 inches of rain fell into an area that was already flooded. Flash Flooding was widespread.
To give some idea of rainfall rates, Ocheyedan received 3 inches in 45 minutes, Allendorf picked up 2.80 inches in just 30 minutes.
Rainfall was intense in Dickinson and Emmet Counties. During a period of 3 to 4 hours, 6.00 to 7.00 inches of rain fell into an area that was already flooded. Flash Flooding was widespread.
A barn was also burn in Emmet County in Independence Township after lightning struck the barn.

The largest hail fell in Emmet County in the Ringsted area. Hail as large as 3.50 inches in diameter pelted the area with many windows reportedly broken out. Reports indicate that north of the Estherville area, baseball-size hail covered the ground.
Lightning struck a mobile home in Cero Gordo County at Rockwell. It was set on fire, completely destroying it.
In Palo Alto County at Ruthven... lightning struck a house. The chimney was knocked off of the house and one wall of the house was bowed after the incident.
In Palo Alto County at Ruthven, grain bins were destroyed by high winds...

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several tornadoes were spawned during the evening. Most of them were brief touch downs and caused little damage. Such was the case in Greene County, where two brief touch downs occurred in open countryside. An earlier touch down north of Sibley, in Ocseola County, did little more than cause tree damage. Two tornadoes touched down in Pocahontas County. The first was a brief touch down. The second was on the ground between Havelock and Gilmore City. Much of the area it traversed was open country. A few farmsteads were affected with most damage to out buildings. One farmstead received significant damage northwest of Gilmore City just before the tornado lifted. The storm was still strong as it moved across the city. Damage was substantial at a lumber yard as high winds lifted the roof from the building and threw it into a house across the street. The lumber yard building was virtually destroyed it. The longest tornado track cut across three counties. The tornado touched down in Boone County and cut a path across southern Story County into northeast Polk County. This tornado had a very intermittent track and lifted several times or remained just above ground. As it moved across northeast Polk County, the storm weakened. Damage was limited due to its intermittent track and the fact that that part of the state is not heavily populated. The storm moved into Jasper County, but by then was below severe levels and just produced heavy rainfall and some small hail. During the late night hours, two tornadoes touched down in Scott County. One north of New Liberty was only a brief touch down and caused no significant damage. The second was north of the Stockton area. A couple was camping in Scott County north of Stockton. The tornado rolled their mobile home. The husband received several cuts and bruises. His wife sustained a broken arm and cuts that required 24 stitches.

A slow moving warm front from eastern Ohio to southwest Pennsylvania triggered thunderstorms which produced heavy rain over southwest Pennsylvania and the Laurel Mountains. From 2100 EDT on the 7th to 0500 EDT on the 8th, thunderstorms continuously developed over extreme eastern Ohio and trained east into Pennsylvania, dumping rain over the same area. Eight-hour rainfall totals included 2.75 inches at Penn Hills, 2.27 inches at Amnity, 2.30 inches at Kingston, 2.15 inches at New Lexington, and 1.92 inches at Berlin. Minor stream flooding was observed. Several reports were received of basement and street flooding.

Current passed through the ground, blowing a hole in the basement wall. It exited via a gas line along side the house where it ripped a garden hose in half and blew a small crater in the dirt. The percussion from the explosion smashed windows and knocked dishes off shelves. Pictures were knocked off walls five lots away.
Near Exit 5 of Interstate 80, two powerpoles were snapped as the result of flying debris from Thunderstorm wind. Trees were also downed in Patchel Run, Barkeyville, Wyattville and Hannaville.

Winds of 70 mph with large flying debris was reported by a Skywarn observer.

The combination of straight line wind and a weak tornado was responsible for damage to several communities in Cambria County. From Spinaly City to Coupon (approximately 3 miles), there was a 1-mile-wide area of wind damage. Structural damage occurred to several homes along with widespread tree damage.

A distinct path of damage was noted from the St. Josephs Cemetery to just east of the community of Coupon. One resident said he saw trees flying through the air, with one tree flying right over the top of his house. A total of twenty residences were damaged. One swimming pool and a small shed were completely destroyed.

A severe hailstorm deposited several inches of hail in southwest Westmoreland County. Between $10,000 and $15,000 in damage was done to the Martins, Flower and Shrub Greenhouses in Rostraver Township. Four greenhouse coverings were destroyed along with numerous plants. Apples were knocked off trees and many gardens were stripped of foliage. The hail which covered the ground took 2.5 hours to melt. Largest hailstones were around 1.50 inches in diameter.

Numerous trees were downed across the county downing powerlines and blocking roads. In Huntingdon, 1.00-inch hail was reported, and a locust tree fell onto a house. There were also reports of street and poor drainage flooding.

From Everson to Wooddale, a tornado destroyed 3 mobile homes and two barns. One of the mobile homes overturned and injured a 45-year-old women. The second mobile home the roof tore off, which landed into a nearby fire station causing $20,000 in damage to the Bullskin Township fire station. A firemen at the station was injured by flying debris. Siding was torn from several other homes, and a porch roof was ripped from a house. A total of 23 homes, 9 mobile homes, 3 barns, a private school, and 1 business received minor damage. Along Route 1047, east of Scottdale, a 1,000 pound horse was seen flying through the air before landing in a nearby creek. The horse underwent surgery for an 8-inch gash to the chest. Five other horses were also fifted off the ground, and carried several hundred yards.
In addition to the 1.00-inch hail report, trees were reported down and there was some urban flooding.

Strong downburst winds caused significant damage to a farm in Shippensburg. The damage included peeling back a metal roof on a hay barn, blowing a 2.25-ton forage wagon on its side, 6 feet from its wheel impression, destroying two hay wagons after blowing them 200 yards, breaking a dozen windows and blowing down a chimney. The winds also split trees vertically and knocked down a utility pole. A fiberglass hutch was blown away with a calf in tow. In other parts of the town, trees were uprooted and power was knocked out. Golfball-size hail also accompanied the storm. Several funnel clouds were spotted with this storm and it is possible that some of the damage may have been caused by an F0 tornado. An investigation of the event; however, indicated that straight line winds were the primary cause of the damage.

Two people were in the structure at the time, but only one person received minor injuries. Several other mobile homes in the park received minor damage. Within 0.25 mile of the mobile home park, an old barn was blown down and three others damaged. Numerous trees were downed in an area that was no more than 200 yards wide and 0.25 mile long. A few houses and hunting cabins were damaged when trees fell on them. All trees, the mobile home and the barn were blown down toward the north. In Williamsport, trees were uprooted. About 1,000 customers lost power throughout the county.
Numerous trees were down near Bentley Creek, Canton and Monroeton from 1145 EST to 1200 EST. Also, funnel clouds were spotted at Athens and Ulster between 1130 EST and 1135 EST.
Spotters reported large trees blown down.
Penny-size hail was reported at Fairhope.
County Emergency Management Agency (EMA) officials reported large trees blown over.
Dime-size hail was reported.
Lightning struck St. John's Evangelical Lutheran Church. The Steeple caught on fire and was so badly damaged that 20 feet of it had to be removed from the church.
Carbon county emergency management reported trees and many large limbs down.

Emergency management and PennDot reported many large limbs down, some power lines down, and several trees uprooted throughout the county. Most damage was in the east section of the county southeast of Allentown. A wind gust of 58 mph was recorded at Allentown Airport.

Police from Easton and the dispatcher from the Northampton county EMA called with reports of trees uprooted as well as many large limbs and wires down throughout the city of Easton and in Wilson borough. Power outages affected 8,300 residents.
Large trees were downed at Somerset.

This small and short-lived tornado was first spotted near North Brandywine JHS and travelled southeast crossing route 30. The tornado veered southwest after crossing route 340 and dissipated in an area east of the Veterans Administration Medical Center. A funnel cloud was spotted aloft during a large portion of the route. The hardest hit area was apparently near Caln. Crews worked through the night to clear dozens of trees and branches, tangled wires, replace fallen utility poles and repair damaged transformers. The hospital was forced to us emergency generator power. Just down the road from the hospital, a barn built in 1812 was turned to rubble. The tornado pushed the silo about 6 inches off its base and collapsed the roof, crushing farm equipment inside. Newly planted crops were blown in all directions and there were 7,000 power outages throughout the county. An AT&T employee was killed when a falling tree struck his vehicle as he was driving north on North Caln Road about 1530 EST. The tree also snapped two electric wires on the way down, preventing rescue workers from getting to the man. (M45V)
Trees were downed and small hail was reported.
Dime-size hail was reported by a weather spotter.

Trees were uprooted, broken and twisted off in all directions. The damage was on top of a hill. An eye witness saw the tornado tear up the trees after heavy rain and half dollar-size hail had moved through the area.

Trees were uprooted, broken and twisted off in all directions. The damage was on top of a hill. An eye witness saw the tornado tear up the trees after heavy rain and half dollar-size hail had moved through the area. At 1715 EST trees were downed 4W of Hop Bottom. An investigation by NWS personnel indicated that it may have been an F0 tornado, but there was no definite confirmation of existence. Additionally, between 1725 EST and 1730 EST, nickel- to quarter-size hail was reported by skywarn observers around Hop Bottom. The general public reported that the hail stripped many local gardens. In Acre Lake an observer reported a driveway was full of hail. No injuries or deaths occurred.
A house sustained an estimated $80,000 worth of fire damage after being struck by lighting.

A small out building was destroyed and the top of a silo was torn off. The front porch collapsed on one house and half the roof was torn off another house and two barns. A few trees were also blown down. The damage to the buildings was almost exclusively located on the south side. All of the debris was blown toward an easterly direction and there was no evidence of any rotation. The damage was caused by a downburst wind estimated to be 60 to 70 knots. An eyewitness said that there was quarter to golfball-size hail between 1740 EST and 1745 EST. An inch or more of hail fell in East Smithfield, followed by 2.00 inches of rain. The hail damaged cornfields and gardens, and on the Berwick Turnpike, a plugged drainage pip funnel a 3-foot pile of hail onto the expressway. One vehicle drove into it. Fortunately, no one was injured.

Numerous trees were downed, and a local resident had a brick and slate chimney blown off of the roof of the house. A large shed was also thrown off its foundation. An investigation by NWS personnel determined that damage was a result of straight line winds.
Large tree limbs and power lines were taken down by the wind. Skywarn observers also reported nickel-size hail.

A 17-year-old boy was struck by lightning at Blairs Corners, while installing a window in a house.

Lightning struck a tree injuring two scouts and three scoutmasters while camping. The group said the lightning felt like it originated from the ground.
Siding and skirting was ripped from several mobile homes in Milesburg. The tops of five pine trees were downed in the same area.

A lightning stroke apparently knocked down power lines behind the Mountainside Manor Personal Care Home on route 309. The 13,000 volt live power lines sizzled on the wet ground, corning into contact with the back of the building and burning through a section of aluminum siding. No injuries were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Sixty-five-mph winds brought large limbs down. The thunderstorm was accompanied by dime-size hail.

Several large trees were blown down.
Three-quarter-inch hail was observed along Route 346, just east of the Allegheny Reservoir.
Trees were downed along State Route 18.
A strong thunderstorm in the vicinity of Mayaguez and Anasco produced heavy rains and hail.
A tropical wave moved across Puerto Rico producing heavy rains over the southeastern sections. Some families were evacuated in Patillas. Road 192 in Naguabo had several areas underwater.

June was unusually hot in South Carolina causing record or near record power consumption. Statewide, it was the driest June of record although isolated severe thunderstorms did occur in some sections of the state. The driest part of the state was across the upper piedmont where many areas reported less than 0.25 inch of rain during the month. Some of the smaller monthly amounts were 0.15 inches at Antreville, Abbeville County, 0.17 inches at Greenville-Spartanburg Airport, and 0.20 inches at Nine Islands in Cherokee County. It was the driest June on record in the Greenville-Spartanburg area. Major crop damage was reported statewide with the corn crop particularly hard-hit.
Lightning killed two valuable horses at Rose Hill Plantation.
Some trees were blown down between Lake City and Johnsonville.
Golf ball-size hail occurred.
Thunderstorm wind and lightning caused considerable minor damage in Conway vicinity. Horry Electric Cooperative reported 400 power outages.
Thunderstorm wind and lightning caused considerable minor damage in Conway vicinity.
A severe thunderstorm moved from Mountain Rest to Walhalla. Falling trees damaged several homes, vehicles, and caused interruptions to power and telephone services.

A severe thunderstorm developed over the western part of Greenville County and moved south through part of the city of Greenville and along the Anderson County border. Trees and power lines were blown down interrupting power for several thousand people in Greenville. Large hail was reported all along the track of the storm before it weakened as it approached the Ware Shoals area.

Thunderstorm wind blew down trees, light pole and damaged several homes in the Sardinia area.
Lightning struck several homes, substations and trees.
Tornado of waterspout origin came from inlet side and tore off or damaged roofs of four homes. Furnishings were smashed against walls and furniture was strewn about by the winds.
Thunderstorm wind blew down several large trees estimated at 200 years old, interrupting power and causing other minor damage.
Lightning-caused fire heavily damaged doctors office.
Eight inches of rain within approximately 4 hours caused minor flooding on several streets including portions of Highway 278. Several homes were evacuated because of the flooding.

Persistant heavy rains caused continued flooding of cropland and rivers, including the Big Sioux and Vermillion, in southeast South Dakota, especially in the latter part of the month after the 22nd. In Sioux Falls, both the 6-month and 12-month periods ending June 30th were the wettest on record with about twice the normal precipitation.
Hail fell in the Norbeck Wildlife Refuge between Hill City and Mt. Rushmore.

An earthquake measuring 4.1 on the Richter scale shook a portion of northeast South Dakota but caused no real damage or injuries. The epicenter of the quake was 22 miles northwest of Morris, Minnesota or 38 miles east of Sisseton, South Dakota and was felt in most of Roberts, Grant, and Deuel Counties in northeast South Dakota. The quake was the first in the area since 1975 and it lasted from 4 to 30 seconds. The quake rattled dishes, knocked down some pictures, made lights swing, and otherwise disturbed people and animals.
Three-quarter-inch-diameter hail was reported between Porcupine and Kyle with 0.50-inch hail occurring at Oglala.
Strong Thunderstorm wind damaged several homes.
Over 3.00 inches of rain flooded some basements and gardens, damaged several area roads, and caused a few dams to run over.

One to three inches of rain caused various problems in the Black Hills. At 1343 MDT, a mudslide caused $15,000 in damage to three vehicles in a Keystone parking lot. The slide carried a large pine tree down a hill into the vehicles and also ripped out telephone and electric lines. The heavy rains caused streams to reach bankfull creating some localized flooding problems. Grizzly Gulch Campground near Keystone was temporariliy evacuated. Several roads were closed due to the high waters, mudslides, or debris. Small creeks flooded some basements and threatened homes south of Pactola Reservoir and near Ellsworth Air Force Base causing some residents to be evacuated.

BEGIN_LOCATION: Lincoln County and N Portion of Clay and Union Counties, and SE Turner County
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hail and heavy rains of up to 3.50 inches inundated an area from northern Clay and Union counties through southeast Turner County to Lincoln County in far southeast South Dakota. The rains caused flooding of basements, roads, and farm fields. In Viborg, 25 homes had up to 2 feet of water in the basements. The downpour also caused urban flooding in Canton shutting down a manufacturing plant.
A boat dock was destroyed by 70-mph winds and resultant waves.

A tornado extensively damaged one farm northeast of Kimball and caused damage to other farms. Several children riding their bicycles in Kimball were picked up by the winds and thrown to the ground causing minor injury.
A tornado ripped out trees and power lines.

A large tornado on the ground for at least 10 minutes destroyed a farmstead. The tornado twisted the house on its foundation virtually destroying it, and destroyed the barn, 3 steel bins, 3 granaries, and 2 hog houses. Ten hogs were also killed. Trees were uprooted and twisted up to a mile north of the farm and pieces of tin roof were wrapped around trees 0.25 mile from the farm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At least three tornadoes touched down in scattered areas of Miner County. In the Fedora area and east of Howard the tornadoes destroyed or damaged farm buildings including barns, sheds, and grain bins. East of Howard a tornado also destroyed a feed elevator and tore the roof off a hog plant. Power lines were knocked down and trees uprooted in some areas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At least three tornadoes damaged several farms in the Tulare and Redfield areas. A tornado hit one farm northwest of Tulare causing about $65,000 in damage. A tornado also damaged a farm 5 miles west of Redfield.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado damaged various buildings and uprooted trees in Farmer. A 18- X 20-foot section of roof was ripped from a church and an old fire hall was flattened. A tornado was also reported 12 miles north of Farmer.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several tornadoes touched down in northern McCook County causing damage to outbuildings on at least 10 farms. Also part of the roof of a bank in Spencer was stripped away. A large tornado that developed northeast of Salem went on to do its most significant damage west of Madison in Lake County.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado destroyed a hog barn on a farm southwest of Broadland and carried the remains nearly a mile.

A large tornado and its attendant vortices left a swath of destruction from northwest Minnehaha County through western Moody County into eastern Brookings County. Numerous farms and residences were destroyed or damaged and trees snapped off or uprooted. Around 1630 CDT multiple vortices formed into the tornado two miles west of Lyons destroying barns and silos and killing animals on several farms. Shortly after, the tornado leveled two houses, seriously injuring four people as they were buried in the rubble. It then caused destruction on at least 10 more farms before entering the northwest side of Colman at 1700 CDT. At least 15 homes in Colman had an estimated total of $250,000 in damage mainly due to the roofs either being blown off or trees falling on them. At 1710 CDT the tornado damaged houses and trees three miles north/northeast of Colman. Around 1715 CDT, 10 miles northwest of Flandreau, the tornado leveled a farm, except for the silo, and injured a man who received multiple pelvis fractures. On two farms, one 2 miles southwest of Aurora and the other 1 mile west of Aurora, buildings and grain bins were destroyed around 1735 CDT. The tornado then continued north/northeast, wrecking irrigation systems and uprooting and snapping off hundreds of trees, before causing destruction on another farm about 6 miles northeast of Brookings around 1745 CDT. Northeast of White, three farms sustained major damage to buildings and trees. Cows were also killed and power lines downed.

A large tornado tore a north/northeast path of destruction through at least 10 farms. On one farm southeast of Junius all that remained was the foundation and steps of the house and the bumper and engine of a pickup truck. On other farms livestock were crippled and a horse was impaled by a piece of wood. At least four people were injured as several vehicles were flipped by the tornado. A woman was driving on a highway west of Madison when the wind started spinning her car around and the windows shattered. About 200 power poles were downed leaving 2800 customers without electricity.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A couple of tornadoes hit farms in the Chester and Wentworth areas. Buildings were damaged or destroyed on farms 2 miles west of Chester, 4 miles northeast of Chester, and north of Wentworth. The tornado blew away an entire residence 2.5 miles north of Wentworth, including the house, garage, and pole shed.

A couple of tornadoes hit farms in the Chester and Wentworth areas. Buildings were damaged or destroyed on farms 2 miles west of Chester, 4 miles northeast of Chester, and north of Wentworth. The tornado blew away an entire residence 2.5 miles north of Wentworth, including the house, garage, and pole shed.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Strong Thunderstorm wind downed trees and power lines and caused minor structural damage in Arlington. A woman received minor injuries from flying glass when a tree crashed through the window of her mobile home.
Thunderstorm wind uprooted trees and caused other minor damage.
Thunderstorm wind gusted to 63 mph at the Watertown Airport.
A tornado was sighted near Clear Lake but no damage was reported.
Hail occurred 4 miles west of Clear Lake.

Strong northerly gradient winds buffeted the Black Hills area downing numerous trees loosened by heavy rains the day before. The trees fell on power lines causing power failures throughout the area. A gust to 60 mph was recorded at the Rapid City Airport at 1319 MDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Tornados and thunderstorms resulted in a destroyed house, several damaged houses and cars, and a few uprooted trees in the Pierre area. A tornado developed as a waterspout over the Missouri River just southwest of Pierre and crossed a baseball field, tossing a van around a parking lot. A tornado moved over a golf course before destroying a house and car as the owner hid in the fireplace. Other smaller tornadoes were reported 15 miles south and east of Pierre. Lightning and hail also occurred in the Ft. Pierre and Pierre area with the hail ranging from marble to baseball size.

A lightning strike is believed to have caused a fire that burned the Keystone Community Hall to its foundation.
A likely tornado tossed two construction trailers and two trucks, and damaged two small buildings. Two men escaped with minor injuries.

Strong outflow winds from dissipating thunderstorms toppled a number of large trees in Bowdle. Winds to 55 mph were reported at Mobridge. Two to five inches of rain also occurred from south of Mobridge to Bowdle with this storm.
High winds destroyed a garage and knocked down trees.
Lightning probably started a fire at a motel causing considerable damage to the office and 11 rooms.
Lightning struck a power line causing power outages in Bushnell and Aurora.
Hail was reported in a 12-mile-long stretch.

Lightning sparked various fires in the Brookings area. A large barn struck by lightning was completely engulfed by the time firefighters arrived. Lightning started a fire at a plant in Brookings around 1935 CDT causing minor smoke damage before fire was controlled. A lightning bolt extensively damaged a Volga house blowing out the inside walls near a chimney and buckling the upstairs floor. Dozens of TV's, VCR's, and other electrical devices were blown out by the lightning in the Brookings area. Heavy rains from the storm caused some flooding of county and township roads.

Heavy rains of 2.00 to 6.00 inches caused renewed flooding in sections of southeast and eastcentral South Dakota. An area extending from Mitchell to Brookings was especially hard hit as flooding affected roads, basements, lakes, creeks, and farmland. Urban flooding occurred in both Mitchell and Brookings. The rain caused Lake Campbell and Lake Hendricks in Brookings County to overflow resulting in some water damage to lakeside homes.
High winds from thunderstorm outflow caused major structural damage to a home and some outbuildings [Note: Event also classified under Hail in original text].
High winds from thunderstorm outflow caused major structural damage to a home and some outbuildings.
A thunderstorm hit Spearfish with high winds, hail, and heavy rains which overflowed gutters.
A severe thunderstorm devastated crops and smashed windows in northeast Meade County with large hail and winds up to 70 mph. The storm also damaged roofs and injured livestock.
Large hail was reported over portions of southern Ziebach County including 10 miles south of Lantry, 14 miles south/southeast of Faith, and 30 miles southwest of Dupree.
Strong Thunderstorm wind destroyed several grain bins and ripped a roof off a building on one farm northwest of Gettysburg.

Tornados and high winds crossed Edmunds County between 2100 CDT and 2200 CDT. At 2100 CDT, the tornado destroyed a building west of Bowdle. The tornado lifted before moving over Bowdle but high winds still toppled trees, one of which crushed a car.
Thunderstorm wind blew the roof off a grandstand in Hoven. Also many trees were broken off and some were uprooted in the Hoven area.
Similar damage occurred in the Roscoe area. West of Roscoe a grain bin was destroyed and a farm building damaged by tornadic winds.
A tornado and high winds damaged buildings on several farms in the Redfield, Athol, and Ashton areas.

A severe thunderstorm moved through the Aberdeen area and caused wind damage especially to the north side of the city. The winds ripped off the roof of a car dealer and also blew out windows and damaged roofs at various businesses.

At 2210 CDT a semi-truck was turned over and crossing signals were destroyed. At 2217 CDT a train boxcar was pushed one block by the wind. Vehicles were damaged by flying rocks. Power lines and trees were also downed by the storm.
A machine shed door was blown off hitting the owner and seriously injuring him. In Hecla, three houses were damaged by falling trees and a grain bin was blown over.

High winds from thunderstorms blew away a 30- X 50-foot farm repair shop on the east side of Pierpont. On the south side of Pierpont, 20 to 30 trees were uprooted damaging some cars and blocking streets. One to three inches of rain caused some flooded basements in Day County.
High winds from thunderstorms gusted to 60 mph in southwest Marshall County causing a barn to collapse 2 miles south of Britton.
Winds pelted a police car with rocks and pea-sized hail. Northeast of Sisseton heavy hail damage to crops was reported.
Wind outflow from thunderstorms destroyed a hog building.
Lightning struck a house and made a hole in the siding. Also electrical appliances in the house were damaged.

Northerly winds gusted to 61 mph at Rapid City Airport at 1612 MDT. A small plane sustained substantial damage when it was flipped by the winds on the runway after landing. The occupants, who were wearing seat belts, were not injured. A few trees were blown over in northern Rapid City and funnel clouds were also reported.
A severe thunderstorm, with large hail driven horizontally by the winds, broke windows and destroyed grain and hay pastures.
Large hail, high winds, and heavy rains struck eastern Todd County devastating crops and washing out pastures. The storm also broke windows and stripped trees and roofs.
Severe storms wiped out some crops and dumped rains up to 2.50 inches in 30 minutes in the Winner area.
Golfball-size hail dented hundreds of automobiles, broke windows, stripped shingles and paint off houses, and pummeled fields around Redfield.
Windows gusting over 50 mph felled hundreds of trees and knocked out power for three hours in Redfield.

A tornado and winds reported at 95 mph destroyed or damaged buildings on at least six farms and downed power lines in the Dixon area. Hail also stripped crops and made the ground white in some locations. Up to 4.00 inches of precipitation was reported, which flooded small streams and stock dams.
Winds in excess of 60 mph uprooted trees.
Winds over 60 mph blew in a barn and caused damage to winter wheat.
Steel bins were blown over and shingles blown off a house.

Winds gusting over 70 mph uprooted trees which fell on vehicles, buildings, and yards. Windows were blown in, scattering glass in several houses. Power was knocked for over 2 hours, and 2.00 inches of rain was measured from the storm.
Heavy rains of 2.00 to 5.00 inches caused flooding mainly of low-lying areas.
Wind gusts to 60 mph downed power lines.
Torrential rains flooded basements, roads, and fields. In the Yale and Cavour areas where the most damage occurred, 4.00 to 8.00 inches of rain was reported.
Strong westerly gradient winds gusting to 65 mph blew over some trees, one of which broke a porch on a house in Buffalo.
High winds near a tornado snapped off large trees, tipped over propane tanks, and tore a roof off a trailer.
Lightning struck a mobile home which resulted in extensive smoke damage.
Baseball-size hail broke out the windows of some cars and houses and damaged small gardens.

A strong tornado crossed the Wyoming/South Dakota border near Cement Ridge and Tinton, South Dakota. Winds of 112 mph were recorded at a nearby lookout tower. The tornado took out a wide swath of large pine trees in the forest on a hillside. Afterwards the U.S. Forest Service had to clear the roads that were full of fallen trees.

Thunderstorm wind blew over trees, some of which fell on houses and power lines. Debris was scattered through the town. Minor street and basement flooding was caused by 1.25 inches of rain in 15 minutes.
Thunderstorm wind destroyed an ultra-light plane on the ground and downed numerous trees and power lines throughout Huron. Branches also fell on cars causing some damage.
Hail knocked windows out of a house and pickup truck and destroyed fields of crops. Also over 4.00 inches of rain caused some flooding with water running over roads.
Hail ranged from pea- to golfball-size.
Heavy thunderstorms brought flooding rains, strong winds, and hail which caused damage to crops in the area. As much as 5.00 inches of rain was reported in northeast Davison County.

The line of thunderstorms blew down a church steeple, tore the roof off of a building and knocked down the back wall of a brick building, blew down an airport hangar, downed trees, damaged buildings, caused approximately 23 injuries, and knocked out power for thousands. Three of the injuries were caused by trees falling on moving cars, the rest were in damaged homes. By 2050 EDT the last damage was reported in the southeastern corner of the state, just south of Norfolk.

The Great Flood of 1993 along the Mississippi River Valley affected Illinois from East Dubuque
to Cairo. As June ended and July began, the Mississippi River continued to rise. The river was
above flood stage at most locations for the entire month of July. Record crests were reached all
along the Illinois border. Significant flooding also occurred along many of the Illinois tributaries
of the Mississippi, including the lower Rock River, the lower Illinois River, the Big Muddy River
and the Kaskaskia River. The Rock River at Joslin and Moline was still about a foot above flood
stage on the last day of July.
On July 9, the Mississippi River at the Quad Cities reached 22.6 feet. This broke the old record
of 22.5 feet set in 1965. River stage records from 1973 along the Mississippi River from Quincy
south were shattered during this flood. The list below gives some of the records as of 7/31/93.
Since the water was still rising, the final record stages were not reached until August.
Flood Stage Record Date Old Record Date
Quincy Illinois: 17 32.2 7/13/93 28.9 4/73
Grafton, Illinois: 18 37.3 7/31/93 33.1 4/73

The flooding put a tremendous strain on many facets of life along and adjacent to the rivers. Not
only were towns and farmland along the rivers affected, but other businesses and people suffered
as well.
Transportation was greatly affected. There are 28 bridges that cross the Mississippi River into Illinois. As of Friday July 16, only 5 were open. The trucking and railroad industries suffered
losses as did people who work on the other side of the river.
Nearly every levee along the Mississippi river, and many along the Illinois river either failed or suffered severe damage. "The cost to repair the levees will go well into the millions.
Barge traffic along the Mississippi was brought to a halt in early July. This meant the loss of an
estimated 1800 jobs and $92 million in revenue a month for the state of Illinois. Total
unemployment in Illinois due to the flood was estimated at 9,000. People of all walks of life came
to the area to help fight the flood. Over 4500 Illinois National Guard Troops were called to duty
to provide security, patrol levees, operate pumps, move materials and fill sandbags. About 400
medium security inmates from various prisons also helped with the sandbagging.
