EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cold front began moving into Iowa from the northwest. Copious amounts of moisture was available for this event with precipitable water values around two inches. Thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon hours. By the early evening the storms had formed into a well developed mesoscale convective system. The main feature with the storms was the heavy rainfall, however there was some severe weather associated with the storms during the event. Golf ball-size hail pelted the area around Schleswig in Crawford County. In fact, baseball-size hail to the south of Schleswig caused total crop destruction in the area. The largest hail reported was in Harrison County at Little Sioux. Hail reached three inches in diameter causing considerable crop damage. In Dow City, also in Crawford County, high winds in what appeared to be a microburst struck. A farm was leveled by winds around 85 MPH. High winds were also reported in Carroll County in the city of Carroll. Minor damage occurred in Decatur City in Decatur County during the decaying stages of the system. There were a few tornadoes spawned by the system. They were each quite small and were only on the ground for a short period of time. One tornado touched down in Crawford County south of Vail. The tornado downed several trees and destroyed a few out buildings. Another tornado touched down near Boone in an open field, causing little damage. A similar situation occurred in Greene County west of Jefferson as well as in Chickasaw County north of New Hampton. One of the storms became rather intense and produced a tornado that was on the ground in Dallas County for several miles. Little damage was reported as the tornado passed between several farmsteads. The same storm cluster later produced a funnel cloud over the northeast part of Des Moines. Reports indicated the funnel was very near touching the ground. Other reports of funnel clouds were received from Cherokee County, where four of them were observed west of Cherokee. A few funnel cloud reports were also received from the surrounding counties, but there were no touch downs. Extremely heavy rainfall was reported in Audubon, Crawford, Carroll, and Greene Counties. Damage was very heavy in Crawford County. Initial reports showed that damage in the county was in the $3-4 million range. Story County was also hard hit as 2 1/2 to 5 inches of rain fell across the Squaw Creek basin. Flooding was severe in Ames, with the creek reaching an all time high. Damage to Iowa State University was in the millions of dollars. The Skunk River also rose markedly, causing additional problems, and eventually closing Interstate 35 fora while. The heaviest rainfall was reported around Coon Rapids with 7.83 inches falling in a few hours time. There were numerous reports of three to seven inch rainfall amounts. Manilla reported 7.50 inches of rainfall, with nearly that amount in Denison. Unofficial amounts were higher. In Greene County, the city of Scranton reported 11 inches of rainfall, while ten inches was reported in Carroll County at Willey. In Crawford County, damage from flash flooding was estimated at $15 million. Severe flood damage occurred in 50 homes in Denison and 36 in Dow City. The water rose so quickly that reports indicated that some homes flooded in as little at 11 minutes. Monona County was also hard hit, with rainfall in the four to nine inch range from Onawa east into Harrison County. Damage was extensive in Shelby County where the flood waters washed out several bridges. Highway 59 was under water two miles south of Defiance. Highway 191 was closed between Earling and Panama by flooding from Mosquito Creek. Two hundred and fifty people were forced out of a mobile home park in Harlan, where the water and sewage plant was flooded. Water ran three feet deep in Irwin. Heavy rainfall in excess of three inches fell across much of the north half of the Raccoon River Basin, and extended into the middle Des Moines River Basin. These rains closed numerous roads and washed out bridges in several counties. At one time the Crawford County sheriff reported that nearly all roads in the county were closed by high water. The heavy rainfall set the stage for what was to become the flood of record along the Raccoon and Des Moines River. Flash flooding also occurred east of this area along much of the line of thunderstorms. The flooding extended on a scattered basis all the way to the northeast part of the state. Some of the heavier rains fell in Tama County. Four inches of rain fell resulting in water in the streets of Tama and Chelsea of seven feet in depth.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Southern Iowa was ahead of the cold front in the warm sector. During the evening hours a Derecho formed over southern Nebraska. The Derecho races across southern Nebraska and southern Iowa at 50 to 60 knots. High winds in the 70 to 100 MPH range were reported with the system. As the storms moved into Iowa, a Bow Echo formed on the lead edge. High winds of 90 to 100 MPH downed 13 high tension power line poles in the eastern part of Council Bluffs. Winds of at least 85 MPH ripped into Fremont County, blowing a church off of its foundation in Bartlett. Considerable tree and building structural damage was reported across the southwest quarter of the state. As an example, roof damage was reported to one house and garage with windows blown in at Pilot Grove Park in Montgomery County, with a shed and barn leveled in Page County near Bethesda. There were two injuries as the storms rolled through. One was south of Glenwood in Mills County as a woman sustained minor injuries from flying debris. Another woman was cut by flying glass near Portsmouth as high winds ripped through the area. Other damage in southwest Iowa included the roof being blown off of a house south of Glenwood and another roof taken off of a mobile home hear Hastings. High winds uprooted trees in Red Oak in Montgomery County. Five miles east of Elliot, a house had windows blown out and damage was done to the roof. As the storms moved into Des Moines, high winds blew car windows out on the south side of the city. High winds in Warren county picked up a gravity bin wagon north of Lacona and threw it 50 feet. A pontoon boat was tossed 100 feet by high winds near Seymour. A few tornadoes were reported. One was actually a gustnado in Monroe County. Several roofs were damaged and tree tops were taken off in the town of Albia. Another tornado touched down briefly north of Agency in Wapello County. A metal building was completely flattened. In what turned out to be one of the stronger tornadoes, a touchdown was reported in the Portsmouth area. Two houses were damaged extensively. In addition, a mobile home was overturned with the roof taken off of another building. A horse trailer was picked up and carried for 250 feet. Rainfall was heavy with the Derecho, but with the speed of movement the amounts were generally less than an inch. Late in the severe weather episode, general river flooding began. The Boyer River flooded through Harrison County from heavy upstream rains. Homes, businesses, and croplands were flooded including areas around Woodbine and Missouri Valley. Seventy five to 80 homes were flooded in Missouri Valley where water was 3 to 4 feet deep in places. The Missouri River also flooded the Willow Creek Area. The West Nishnabotna River flooded through Pottawattamie County. About 50 people were evacuated in Avoca where water flooded the town to the highest levels since 1947. Interstate 80 was closed in the area for a time on the 9th after water swept a number of cars off the roadway. Downstream, record flooding occurred around the Hancock area where the park was heavily damaged. The crest rolled into the Oakland area early on the 10th, overflowing sand bags and flooding widespread areas of the town. Numerous roads were flooded and bridges damaged. Crop damage was heavy. The Missouri River also overflowed, forcing evacuations at Goose Haven and Honey Creek. In Mills and Fremont Counties, the West Nishnabotna River flooded croplands and roads throughout the area, damaging some bridges. Some overflows affected the area around Hastings.

The heavy rainfall event that occurred on the afternoon and evening of the 8th into the early morning of the 9th set the stage for what was to become the flood of the century, or the great floo?
of 1993. Several events took place to cause the major flooding to occur. Heavy rainfall, as much
as 11 inches in places, occurred during the afternoon and evening hours of the 8th. The heaviest
rainfall fell along the upper reaches of the Raccoon River. Heavy rainfall of several inches was reported over almost all of the state during this period. By the afternoon of the 9th, the lake levels
at Lake Panora had risen so rapidly a decision was made to release over three hundred million cubic
feet of water from the lake in a rush that local residents said sounded like the dam had broken.
Another round of rainfall occurred on the morning of the 10th across northern Iowa, adding to an already serious situation. By the 10th, record crests were moving down many of lowa's rivers.
In what added the crowning glory to the flooding, heavy rainfall of two to three inches, with isolated amounts between four and five inches, fell over western and central Iowa at the time the
crest was approaching the area. Record river levels were recorded in many areas. For example,
the Raccoon River crested near seven feet over the all time record crest at the southwest 18th street
bridge. The Des Moines Water Treatment plant on Fleur Drive was inundated by water during the
predawn hours of the 11th. This resulted in the loss of water for 250,000 residents for 12 days,
and stopped the flow of drinking water for 19 days. Water service was lost to many communities
around the state during this period of extreme flooding. Damage around the state was extensive and
well into the billions of dollars. Within a few days of the floods beginning all 99 counties in Iowa
had received the federal disaster declaration. In addition to the record crests on the rivers,
reservoirs around the state reached record levels. Saylorville Reservoir overflowed for the second
time in 1993 and crested around 56 feet over normal pool state. Coralville Reservoir overflowed
for the first time in its history as did Red Rock Reservoir. Rathbun Reservoir overflowed late in
the month. The total dollar damage estimates were nowhere close to being in by the time of this writing. A few estimates had been received on a preliminary basis. The city of Des Moines was
hard hit. At the peak of the flooding, between 30,000 and 35,000 households were without electricity and 50,000 were without power at one time or another during the flood. Water service
was out for 250,000 people, which as mentioned was the largest water outage in United States
history. Losses to the business in the area due to lost business were estimated at $700,000,000.
Other damage in Des Moines included $253 million in physical damage, $30 million in damage to
homes, $100 million in damages to businesses, $75 million to the levee system, and $20 million damage to the water treatment plant. Reports from West Des Moines included 237 businesses
damaged at a cost of $20 million, 685 homes damaged at a cost of $6 million, damage to the streets
and sanitary system was $6 million, and $3 million in damages to city parks. Some examples of damages to more rural areas: In Des Moines County, 250 houses were damaged, 50 businesses damaged, and eight municipal buildings damaged. In Van Buren County damages were estimated around $5 million. Damage occurred to 165 homes and ten mobile homes. Thirteens homes were destroyed. Eighty one businesses were damaged, three of which were destroyed. Thirty four miles
of roads were severely damaged. Four hundred homes had to be evacuated. There were two flood
related injuries in Van Buren County as a couple was trapped in their basement by the rising water.
The husband sustained a broken arm, his wife sustained superficial wounds. Reports like these
were filed for nearly every county in the state. A complete report is beyond the scope of this
report. There were four people hospitalized in lowa City as bacteria crept into the water supply. The flooding was extensive with hundreds of roads closed around the state. Many of the interstates
were closed at times as well. Interstate 380 was closed as the water from the Coralville Reservoir
overtopped the roadway. Interstate 80 was closed by the Raccoon, Des Moines, and Skunk Rivers.
Interstate 35 was closed by the Skunk and Raccoon Rivers. Crop damage was extensive as well.
Many areas were under water for extended periods of time, destroying crops. Reports indicated
that 6.5 million acres of cropland were damaged by this flood alone.
The West Nishnabotna River flooded through Pottawattamie County. About 50 people were evacuated in Avoca... Interstate 80 was closed... Downstream, record flooding occurred around the Hancock area.
In Mills and Fremont Counties, the West Nishnabotna River flooded croplands and roads throughout the area, damaging some bridges.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms fired up across northern Iowa in a very moist and unstable atmosphere. They were ahead of an approaching cold front. The storms fired during the early afternoon hours. They tracked across northern Iowa into the east-central counties. A few tornadoes were spawned by the stronger storms. One touched down briefly in Cerro Gordo County. The second touched down in Floyd County. This tornado was on the ground for about 12 mifes and caused damage to a few farmsteads. For the most part the storms caused high winds, at times gusting to around 80 MPH. Winds gusted to 80 MPH in Ogden, in Boone County. Numerous reports of trees and power lines being downed by the high winds were received. Early in the storms development, large hail was reported in northwest Iowa. Baseball and larger size hail fell in Lyon and Sioux Counties with a swath of 90% crop damage from northwest to southeast of Boydon. All of the windows on the north side of the houses in Boydon were broken by the hail. Other reports of hail were received after these initial reports. Most of the hail was pea to marble-size. Three-quarter inch diameter hail fell in Winneshiek County at Decorah, while the largest hail report was in Webster County. Callender reported golf ball to softball-size hail briefly. Crops were destroyed and leaves stripped off of trees in the area. The combination of the hail and three inches of rainfall caused large drifts of hail. High winds resulted in an injury in Floyd County. An 11 year old was injured at a campground as a tree branch fell on his leg. In Palo Alto County, lightning struck a golf cart shed at a local golf course. It started a fire that destroyed the shed and several carts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The synoptic situation was set up a little differently than that of the past several days. The warm front had moved north into Iowa, however several old outflow boundaries remained from the past days convection. There were three main differences in the pattern on this day as compared with the previous several. The first was that a strong low level jet became established during the evening. What was on the order of 30 kts by late afternoon increased to 50 to 60 kts during the evening. This was stronger than the low level jet of the past several days. A cold front was approaching, which also aided in the formation of convection. The third factor was a strong short wave, or upper air disturbance, approaching the area. These factors combined to set of explosive thunderstorm development during the late afternoon hours into the evening. The storms first fired up over southeast Nebraska. The storm cluster expanded into a mesoscale convective complex in just three hours time as the low level jet pushed a pool of 75 to 80 degree dew point temperatures into the region. The storms produced copious rainfall over parts of Nebraska. During the early evening a strong line developed on the lead edge of the complex. This line advanced into lowa at nearly 50 kts. This spared lowa of what could have been a flooding/flash flooding event of historical proportions. The speed of movement kept precipitation amounts under two inches in most areas. Heavy rainfall of two inches in a 30 minute time me period was reported in Council Bluffs area. Streets were flooded with numerous intersections under water. A theater was damaged when flood waters crept in. About two feet of water covered the theater's parking lot. The storm complex was tornadic as it moved across southeast Nebraska. Two tornadoes were spawned in southwest Iowa. The first straddled the Mills and Fremont County line south of Glenwood. It was preceded by two funnel cloud reports in Fremont County about 20 minutes prior to touchdown. The tornado damaged trees and caused considerable damage to a mobile home east of Bartlett. The main feature with the storms was high winds. A few funnel clouds were reported over southwest Iowa during the early stages of the event. They were reported in both Page and Adams Counties. A small tornado touched down briefly in the town of Corning about an hour before. The funnel cloud came from a secondary storm that developed. Heavy rainfall that began in late June became more persistent and widespread during July causing severe, significant and in some areas record setting flooding. Rainfall amounts during July of 8 to 18 inches were common with some areas along the Nebraska border picking up 20 to 24 inches. Most rainfall fell during the first three weeks of the month and ended in many areas by the 27th. The rainfall coupled with saturated soil and eventually large discharges from completely filled Corp of Engineers reservoirs produced flooding along every river, stream and creek across the area. Even on days when rains did not occur rivers remained in flood or very high as water flowed into them from the swollen lakes and reservoirs. Scattered thunderstorms produced areas of flash flooding during the month especially from July 17th to the 25th. The Flood of '93 as it was called was compared to the record setting Flood of 1951 both in areas covered and magnitude. However, due to flood control levees and reservoirs, flooding in 1993 was not as damaging nor deadly. Flooded farmland was eastimated at 75,000 to 100,000 acres. The Kansas River at Topeka crested at 34.8 ft, the highest in 20 years, at Manhattan at 30.0 ft, while the Big Blue River at Blue Rapids crested at a record 63.1 ft nearly 40 ft above flood stage. Property and crop damage only in northeast Kansas was estimated at $30 to $40 million.

This event actually began in June and continued through July 31. The flooding that began in the latter half of June continued into July as heavy precipitation coninued and runoff increased. As these heavy rains continued, virtually every low lying or flood prone area had begun to fill with water and persons flying over the area said that the whole region looked more like a giant lake. Floodwaters continued to rise, more homes and businesses had to be evacuated and more roads and bridges had to be closed from either being washed away or flooded. In almost all areas, water levels were at an all time high and there seemed to be no end in sight. Several major reservoirs got so full that in spite of the effects on the ongoing flood situation, water had to be released for fear of dam breakage. By the third week in July, the heavy rains had subsided, but due to the backwaters and excessive flooding downstream, water levels did not drop below flood stage until the 31st.

The combination of runoff from thunderstorms over the upper reaches of the Missouri River basin and repeated heavy rains over the local region, sent the Missouri and Kansas Rivers to historic heights. Record crests were set at most locations along the Missouri River, including Atchison, Kansas (est 30.7 ft on 7/15/93). Many of the sites set records during the of the month, and then reset even higher crests towards month's end. The Kansas River also spent much of the month well above flood stage, being heavily influenced by record crests on the Missouri River. The river crested at De Soto at 26.97 ft on 7/28/93 while at Kansas City it crested at 54.97 ft on 7/28/93. Approximately 60,000 acres of crops were affected by the flooding in Doniphan, Johnson, Leavenworth and Wyandotte counties. The Missouri flooding forced more than 1000 people to evacuate in Elwood, Kansas where a levee was topped. Fifteen hundred people were flooded out of their homes in Wyandotte County, and another 3500 families were evacuated as a precautionary measure from an area where the Kansas and Missouri Rivers converge in Kansas City, Kansas. Damage to roads, bridges, and homes along the flooded rivers were estimated at nearly $10 million throughout the 4 county area. The event lasted all month with waters finally falling below flood stage in early August.

This event began around 2000 CST on 7/1/93 and continued through 7/31/93. As the heavy rain pattern began to spread across the Western portions of Central Kansas during the last week of June, the ground became saturated and the area creeks, rivers, and tributaries were on the rise. During the evening of July 1, three to six inch rainfalls were reported across portions of this area caused massive flooding to begin. From this point on, heavy rainfalls continued on a fairly regular basis which kept water at record high levels. In addition to the rainfall, water continued to back into this area due to the excessive flooding downstream. This combination kept water levels at or above flood stage the entire month. Like the flooding across the rest of Central and North Central Kansas, numerous homes and businesses had to be evacuated as severe and extensive damage was being inflicted upon buildings, roadways, and farmsland. Numerous roads and bridges had to be closed and many fields were so full of water they looked like shallow lakes. The heavy rains began to let up in the third week of July, but due to the excessive flooding elsewhere and the backwaters associated with it, water levels did not drop below flood stage until the 31st.

A Bermuda High set up off the east coast of the United States pumping a southerly flow of hot and humid air into the Northeastern United States. Daytime highs across eastern New York were in the 90s to around 100 in most areas with overnight lows from the mid 60s to mid 70s through the period. The rainfall for July was much above normal for all of North Dakota. Monthly amounts ranged from five to ten inches over most of the state. However, the National Weather Service Office in Bismarck recorded 13.75 inches of rain, an all-time monthly record. In the town of Wilton, 20 miles north of Bismarck, 16.81 inches of rain fell during the month. The heavy rains caused major urban flooding in the cities of Bismarck, Mandan, Jamestown, Valley City, Devils Lake, Grafton and and Fargo. Small towns, such as Glen Ullin and Fessenden, and rural communities were also affected. Many rivers and streams reached record high stages. Total damage was over $406,000, mostly to crops, and many farmers were unable to plant their flooded fields. Many highways, roads and railroad tracks were washed out. On July 21, Governor Ed Schafer declared the entire state a disaster area, due to the worst flooding ever. The excessive rains, cloudy skies, and cool weather, hurt tourism and outdoor recreation.

A persistent ridge of high pressure centered over the southeast and extending northward well into the Middle Atlantic region began a heat wave that lasted eleven days. The searing daytime heat, followed by humid nights offering no relief, resulted in numerous deaths-- especially in Philadelphia. This heat wave claimed over one hundred lives in Philadelphia /107/, most of which apparently occurred over the weekend of the 9th and 10th. The number of deaths related to this heat wave was the most ever in Philadelphia, however, this number was highly controversial and partially a result of a campaign to educate the public about preventable deaths among the frail elderly. The overwhelming majority of the deaths were among people 60 years and older. In too many cases, the victims had been shuttered away in the upstairs of intercity apartments with no fan or air conditioner. In Philadelphia, there were nine days of 95 or above temperatures during the heat wave. July 2nd to July 4th marked three consecutive days with a temperatures of 100 degrees or more. Aside from the fatalities related to the excessive heat, several concrete roads buckled and/or exploded, crops were scorched, and livestock were less productive. The actual extent of damage is difficult (if not impossible) to estimate.

Area lakes including Pickerell, Blue Dog, Enemy Swim, and Buffalo lakes rose over two feet, inundating areas around lake homes, submerging docks, and setting boats adrift. One of the driest July's on record prevailed over north Texas in 1993. At many locations (including Fort Worth and Waco),no rain was reported in July for the first time since records began (going back nearly a hundred years). By the end of the month,many crops were reported suffering from the lack of rain. Brush and grass fires were increasing in frequency,including one that burned 4000 acres of ranch land in Young county and another that burned 2800 acres in Palo Pinto county. The Texas Forest Service declared the eastern two-thirds of the state (some 50 million acres) was in extreme fire danger,and by the end of month,many counties had banned outdoor burning. Water supply was only a problem in a few rural areas,as most lakes and reservoirs were full from spring rains. However,water and electric usage was setting records in many locations by the end of the month.

At least two roofs were blown off by winds that the public estimated at 90 MPH.
Winds estimated at 60 MPH occurred on Highway 349 north of Rankin.
The public reported 60 MPH winds 14 miles north of Midkiff in eastern Midland County.
A severe thunderstorm produced a powerful microburst which damaged hangar doors and uprooted trees at the Pecos Airport. The Texas Department of Public Safety estimated the peak wind at 105 MPH.

Isolated severe thunderstorms produced hail up to nickel-size and winds up to 70 miles an hour in north Texas during the evening hours on the 17th. Strong Thunderstorm wind blew the roof off a barn two miles east of Holliday.
The Odessa Police Department reported flooding which submerged an underpass as well as some service roads in east Odessa.
A mobile home was blown across Highway 87 and destroyed by strong Thunderstorm winds between Wall and Vancourt.
The Sterling County Sheriff's Office reported winds in excess of 60 MPH in Sterling City. Pea-size hail accompanied the storm.
Approximately 100,000 chickens reportedly died from excessive heat.
Texas DPS and Tulia PD reported nickel-size hail in Tulia.
Tree limbs were reported downed around the city.
Tree limbs were reported downed in the area.
The San Jacinto County Sheriff's Office reported a tornado on Highway 190 between Oakhurst and Point Blank. Roofs blown off and trees uprooted in the Waterhood subdivision.

The Fort Bend Emergency Management reported golf ball-size hail near Katy at 1750 CST, golf ball-size hail in Katy and in Fulshear and on Westheimer Boulevard west of Highway 8 at 1815 CST. A gazebo was blown over, small signs were blown down, and shutters were blown off buildings across northern Fort Bend County from a downburst from this thunderstorm.
Microburst wind in Perryton broke several large tree limbs and damaged a park pavilion when a picnic table designed for 30 people was blown several yards out of the pavilion.

Strong and gusty northwest winds developed behind a cold front that had moved through northwest Utah. Peak wind gusts ranged from 60 to 64 mph. Some minor damage occurred in Eureka in extreme northeast Juab County.
Thunderstorms developed along an old frontal boundary. Because of the dry lower levels, these thunderstorms produced very strong microbursts.

Additional thunderstorms developed along the previously mentioned frontal boundary. The Utah Highway Patrol reported the microburst winds in the Holden and Flowell areas. These towns are north and west of Fillmore in the eastern portion of the county. The microbursts blew down several trees. These thunderstorms moved east, and weakened shortly thereafter.
An area of thunderstorms moved through northern Utah. These storms produced strong and gusty winds. Gusts up to 61 mph were reported.
The above mentioned thunderstorms continued to move east and produce the gusty winds. The winds knocked down several power poles at Midway in the northwest portion of the county.

The previously mentioned thunderstorms continued to move east and produce more gusty winds. In the Tridell area,area,several large tree limbs were blown off. In the Vernal area,the wind damaged power lines in addition to blowing down trees. Blowing dust also reduced the visibility to near zero at times.

Thunderstorms developed along a slow moving cold front. Because of the slow moving front and a southwest flow aloft, one thunderstorm after another moved through the Wasatch Front area from the late afternoon hours of the 25th through the mid-morning hours of the 26th. These storms produced frequent lightning. One of the bolts hit a swing set in the back yard of a residence in Orem. The bolt went into the ground, and blew out patches of the lawn and part of a small concrete retaining wall. The electric current then entered the house where it damaged a television and vcr.

More lightning produced from the above mentioned thunderstorms hit three different locations approximately at the same time. In Sugarhouse, the lightning hit the roof of a house, and instantly set the house on fire. The fire gutted the attic, and burned through the second floor ceiling. Damage was estimated at $50,000. In Salt Lake City, the lightning hit the chimney of a house, went down a drain pipe, and started a fire that caused $50,000 damage. In Sandy, lightning hit a motor for a heater/ventilation system on a building housing a medical-equipment manufacturer. Power was knocked out, and fumes from the system were released into two offices. These thunderstorms also produced locally heavy rainfall which caused some minor urban flooding.

Thunderstorms developed over portions of southwest Utah. One of these storms produced strong microburst winds in the Richfield area. The wind caused tree damage, and blew a camper trailer and some horse stalls over. No speeds were available.

A Bermuda High set up off the east coast of the United States pumping a southerly flow of hot and humid air into the Northeastern United States. Daytime highs were 90 to 95 in most areas with overnight lows from the mid 60s to mid 70s through the period.
Severe Thunderstorm wind downed numerous trees and power lines in Plainfield and Marshfield during the late afternoon hours of July 8th.

Severe thunderstorms formed and moved along a stationary front which was anchored across central Vermont. Thunderstorm wind downed trees and power lines across parts of the state with the roof blown off a barn in Danby. In West Barnet a tree fell on a car injuring one of its occupants.

Severe thunderstorms moved through parts of Orleans County ahead of a cold front on the evening of the 20th. Thunderstorm wind blew two silage wagons across a field, through two fences and into a manure pit in Newport Center. In Barton inch diameter hail and 2.00 inches of rain fell in a 15 minute period.

Severe thunderstorms occurred over northwest Vermont as a strong northwesterly flow swept across the area. Thunderstorm wind downed trees and nickel-size hail fell in Westford and dime-size hail fell in Milton.

A strong cold front swept through Vermont late on the 29th resulting in severe thunderstorms across parts of the state. Thunderstorm wind downed trees, tree limbs and power lines with the areas hardest hit being Addison, Caledonia and Windham Counties. In West Dummerston a wet microburst caused extensive damage to a house and a garage with at least 200 trees down in an area 200 yards wide by 1/2 mile long. Other areas hard hit included Groton, Ferrisburg, and between Middlebury and Bristol. In Groton at the Stillwater campground a family of six was tent trailer camping when three trees came down on their camper. They sought refuge in their van until another tree came down across the windshield. All six were sent to the hospital with minor injuries. Ice cube-size hail was also reported in Groton. Numerous large trees and power lines were downed in Ferrisburg, and along Route 116 between Middlebury and Bristol.
A pilot observed a waterspout 7 miles west of St. Thomas airport.
A July heat wave and dry period caused large amounts of damage to corn crops in southeast Virginia.
A 28 year old man was injured by lightning while talking on the phone.
A woman received a shock from a nearby lightning strike while she was taking clothes from a clothes line during a thunderstorm.

A band of thunderstorms brought strong winds and nickel-sized hail to the Richmond area and southern Virginia. A few trees were knocked down. However, only lightning strike property damage was reported.
A band of thunderstorms passed through northwestern Virginia knocking down trees but not causing any reported property damage.
A powerful summertime thunderstorm produced golf ball-sized hail which shattered a skylight at the Greenbriar Mall.

Two bands of thunderstorms developed as a cold front passed through the mid-Atlantic. Strong winds were reported in many counties throughout the region causing widespread but fairly minor damage. he most intense weather related event was in western Loudoun county where downburst Thunderstorm wind were estimated at 95 mph and a small weak tornado moved through downtown Leesburg. Damage from the tornado was mostly downed trees and tree limbs with some damage
to roof tops.
The other tornado occurred approximately two miles southeast of the town of Stafford, in Stafford County. This was a very small and weak tornado and touched down briefly. It damaged a small boat and an RV at one residence, blew the window out of one house, knocked down several trees and took the some shingles off of a couple of houses.
Pea-size hail was reported in many areas and rainfall rates exceeded three inches per hour in many of the storms.
Strong Thunderstorm wind knocked down a few trees in parts of Central Virginia.
A isolated summertime thunderstorm knocked down a few trees in Highland county.

Western Virginia was pounded by a band of thunderstorms that created winds in excess of 55 knots in a few locations. The most intense storm was one that had developed in the panhandle of West Virginia and proceeded to move into northwest Virginia.

A heavy rain shower that remained stationary over Everett, caused some minor flooding. A home was damaged when water rushed down a hill and poured into the basement for 45 minutes. Also, a car stalled when it drove into a four-foot deep pool of water on Airport Road.
An evening hail storm damaged approximately 50 acres of apples. The hail was described as being small, but the damage was estimated at $225,000

High winds from a strong thunderstorm caused a variety of damage in the city. Windows were blown out of three businesses in downtown and a large billboard and marquee were blown down. Three large trees and a power pole were also blown over. A wind gust to 46 mph was recorded at the Grant County Airport, located five miles northwest of the city.

A funnel cloud was reported by the Adams County sheriff at Hatton, about 30 miles southeast of Ritzville. At approximately the same time, a deputy reported near zero visibility in blowing dust along highway 26, between Othello and Wastucna.
Power was lost in the southern half of the county when a lightning strike knocked a 115,000 volt transmission line structure to the ground.

Thunderstorms with heavy rain, flooded streets and caused erosion around the city's waste water treatment plant. Local highways were shut down for two hours due to mud and debris flows up to three feet deep.

A thunderstorm cut a three to five mile swath from the Brodix area east through Creston. Hail measuring up to one inch and flash floods, damaged or destroyed thousands of acres of wheat with an estimated yield of of 60 to 80 bushels per acre. The Grand Coulee highway and several other area roads were covered by mud and rock slides. Three large trees were blown down in Creston.
About 300 acres of Red Delicious apples were damaged by a hail storm that lasted 30 minutes. Damage was estimated at 80 percent of the crop, for a loss of 1.1 million dollars.
A funnel cloud was reported near Graham that lasted about 90 seconds.
A tree was blown down in the town of Ione by strong Thunderstorm wind.

Three lightning strikes within minutes of each other, damaged homes and injured a 27 year old woman in Auburn. The woman was knocked across the room while setting a clock radio. The strike also blasted a 12 inch hole in the side the house and burnt out the electrical system., The other two homes, one in Auburn the other in Kent, also suffered blast and electrical system damage.

Stationary thunderstorms dumped very heavy rain over King and south Snohomish counties from Auburn to Brier. The rains flooded streets with one to two feet of water and prompted the closing of several ramps leading to Interstate 405. Several homes and businesses in the area area also were damaged due to flooding and mud flows. Storm totals ranged from one over three inches. The most extreme report was received from a forest service employee who recorded 3.20 inches of rain in 30 minutes. Power was also knocked out to 9,000 customers due to lightning strikes.
A report from the public indicated that two funnel clouds were located over the west edge of Lake Washington in south Seattle.

Many streets in Spokane were flooded with water from one half to three feet deep, as a result of heavy rain from a thunderstorm. There were also a few homes and businesses that experienced minor flooding. Hail as large as three-quarter inch was also reported with the rain.

Two flood waves hit Wilbur, flowing down Goose Creek and its drainage ditches. The first wave flowed down Goose creek, ripping out a small wooden dam. Just as this was receding, another more powerful flood roared down a drainage ditch from the north. This flood spread out to 75 to 100 feet wide, flooding several garages and workshops.
A farmer, three and a half miles southwest of Edwall, lost some wheat due to flooding. The Lincoln County sheriff also reported serious flooding near Blue Stem, about ten miles south of Davenport.

Many streets in Spokane were flooded with water from one half to three feet deep, as a result of heavy rain from a thunderstorm. There were also a few homes and businesses that experienced minor flooding. Hail as large as three-quarter inch was also reported with the rain.

A storm cell developed over south Grant County overnight and barely moved for the next nine hours. One to two inches of rain was measured with one location receiving 0.90 inch of rain in one hour. Roads were flooded or washed out in southern Grant County and near Royal City, in Adams County.

At least 2.50 inches of rain from a thunderstorm caused flooding of homes and fields in and around Ritzville. The Fire Chief received numerous calls on flooded basements. One home had water running through it nearly as high as the first floor windows. Large equipment was also reported as being washed down gullies.

Two heat waves,from the 4th to the 11th and from the 24th to the 28th,curtailed many outdoor activities. The ground quickly dried out as showers were infrequent and scattered. Preliminary data indicated that the average monthly temperature at Bluefield was the second hottest for any July and the third hottest for any month since 1891. At Beckley,the month was the hottest and driest July since the weather station opened in 1963. At Elkins,it was the fourth hottest and fourth driest July since 1899. At Charleston,the month was the second driest July and the fifth hottest July this century. The 100 degrees at Charleston on the 28th was the hottest temperature since the summer of 1988 in that city. Power companies reported new summertime peak demands for electricity. One vacationer was treated at a hospital,when she was overcome by the heat. By month's end some farmers were hauling water for livestock or selling off their stock.

Monthly rainfall of 4 to over 14 inches over southern and central Wisconsin continued the flooding problems of the previous month. The Mississippi River,at least seven major rivers,many smaller streams and tributaries,and numerous lakes overflowed their banks during the month. The Pecatonica River basin in south-central Wisconsin received the brunt of the rainfall and worst flooding. A record flood occurred at Blanchardville (Lafayette County) with near record flooding at Darlington (Lafayette County) and Martintown (Green County). The Fox River near Berlin (Green Lake County) and Pecatonica River at Martintown remained above flood stage all month. Much of downtown Darlington was flooded along with parts of Blanchardville as the Pecatonica crested on July 6th. Damage resulting from the widespread flooding was mainly in crop losses. Since the rain and flooding began in the spring,crop and infrastructure damage estimates by county included Jackson $50 million,Lafayette $10.5 million,Adams $10 million,Juneau $9 million,Green $7 million,Waupaca $6 million and Columbia $4 million. By the end of July,39 counties were declared federal disaster areas. Overall damage this agricultural season affected 2.25 million acres,totalling $525 million,with $450 million from flooding and excessive rains,and $125 million from winter-kill of 750,000 acres of alfalfa. Over 56,000 farmers were affected by these weather conditions. When losses from reduced yields are added,the estimated total crop loss would be near $1 billion. The flooding continued to affect tourism,outdoor activities,construction and sporting events.

Slow moving thunderstorms dumped from 12 to 13 inches of rain in four hours on the Baraboo River and Skillet Creek near Baraboo (Sauk County). As a result,a killer flash flood developed causing about $8 million damage to Baraboo and nearby Devils Lake State Park. A 12 year old boy drowned when the car in which he was riding was lifted by the current, struck by a tree, and landed in a culvert. He drowned when he became trapped in the car by water and debris. Numerous roads were washed out,people were stranded on roof tops,homes and businesses flooded,cars swept away and bridge washed out. Nearly $200,000 in damage occurred when the nearby Devils Lake State Park grounds flooded out. Damage in Baraboo included 11 businesses ($4.9 million), several residences ($360,000), and public infrastructure ($2.5 million). (M12V)
